title: Counting and Painting Chromosomes
endLine: Stained spreads and fluorescent probes expose chromosome number, rearrangements, and territories.

scenes.tts: How do you count chromosomes and spot swapped pieces inside a crowded nucleus? Chromosomes live there in pairs, one homolog from each parent. Karyotyping uses stained spreads to count and match them. Fluorescent DNA probes that bind matching sequences, a method called fish, make chosen chromosomes glow.
scenes.caption: How do you count chromosomes and spot swapped pieces inside a crowded nucleus? Chromosomes live there in pairs, one homolog from each parent. Karyotyping uses stained spreads to count and match them. Fluorescent DNA probes that bind matching sequences, a method called FISH, make chosen chromosomes glow.
scenes.visual: A dark schematic cell nucleus filling most of the frame height, crowded with gently drifting tangled chromatin strands; as the opening question settles, the title 'Counting and Painting Chromosomes' appears briefly and clears; inside the same nucleus, paired homolog outlines emerge, then split into two preview cues: banded rods on the left and glowing fluorescent labels on the right (all schematic).
scenes.narration: How do you count chromosomes and spot swapped pieces inside a crowded nucleus? Chromosomes live there in pairs, one homolog from each parent. scenes.tts: First, catch a dividing cell in mitosis, when each chromosome packs into a compact rod. Spreading and staining those rods lets you count every chromosome. In people, the usual count is forty-six. The stain leaves stripes, called bands. Sorting rods by size and banding matches homologous pairs, forming a karyotype.
scenes.caption: First, catch a dividing cell in mitosis, when each chromosome packs into a compact rod. Spreading and staining those rods lets you count every chromosome. In people, the usual count is 46. The stain leaves stripes, called bands. Sorting rods by size and banding matches homologous pairs, forming a karyotype.
scenes.visual: Continuing from the same schematic nucleus: entering mitosis, the tangled strands condense into compact banded rods; the nuclear boundary opens and the stained rods fan out flat across the frame; a live counter ticks to 46 as rods pulse in turn; the rods then glide smoothly into matched homologous pairs ordered by size, labelled 'Karyotype (schematic)'.
scenes.narration: First, catch a dividing cell in mitosis, when each chromosome packs into a compact rod. Spreading and staining those rods lets you count every chromosome. scenes.tts: To track one chromosome, add fluorescent DNA probes that stick to its matching sequence. Labelling whole chromosomes in colour is chromosome painting. After mitosis, each chromosome partly unpacks, yet keeps its own space, a chromosome territory. Stained spreads and fluorescent probes turn a nucleus into countable pairs, traceable pieces, and mapped territories.

scenes.visual: On the same schematic karyotype spread, bright fluorescent probes sweep across the rods and light selected homologous pairs in vivid distinct colours; the spread then folds back into a post-mitosis nucleus where each painted chromosome partly unpacks into a soft glowing patch filling its own region, labelled 'Chromosome territories (schematic)', with gentle ambient drift inside each territory.

scenes.tts: Now test what a chromosome count alone can tell you. Suppose a stained spread shows forty-six chromosomes, the usual count. Does that normal count rule out extra chromosome twenty-one DNA, or a disrupted gene?
scenes.caption: Now test what a chromosome count alone can tell you. Suppose a stained spread shows 46 chromosomes, the usual count. Does that normal count rule out extra chromosome 21 DNA, or a disrupted gene?
scenes.visual: The painted nucleus opens back into the schematic stained spread with a high-contrast readout reading '46 chromosomes'; pair 21 gently pulses; a clear question card appears above the spread: '46 chromosomes: normal DNA and genes?' while slow ambient shimmer keeps the spread alive.
scenes.narration: Now test what a chromosome count alone can tell you. Suppose a stained spread shows 46 chromosomes, the usual count. Does that normal count rule out extra chromosome 21 DNA, or a disrupted gene?

scenes.visual: Deliberate thinking pause: the question card '46 chromosomes: normal DNA and genes?' stays on screen above the 46-chromosome schematic spread while a calm slow highlight glides across the pairs without revealing the answer.

scenes.tts: No, count is only the first clue. A cell with forty-six chromosomes can still hold extra chromosome twenty-one material, attached to another chromosome. A swap, called a translocation, can place a gene beside another gene's strong control region without changing total DNA. And a tumor's two copies of chromosome thirteen can both carry one mutant gene version, leaving no normal copy.
scenes.caption: No, count is only the first clue. A cell with 46 chromosomes can still hold extra chromosome 21 material, attached to another chromosome. A swap, called a translocation, can place a gene beside another gene's strong control region without changing total DNA. And a tumor's two copies of chromosome 13 can both carry one mutant gene version, leaving no normal copy.
scenes.visual: The question clears as fluorescent colour exposes three hidden cases on the same schematic spread: first, a bright chromosome-21 segment glows attached to another rod while the counter still reads 46; second, two chromosomes swap coloured tips to illustrate a translocation placing a gene beside a glowing strong control region of another gene with total length unchanged; third, both rods of pair 13 stay intact yet turn the same mutant colour, showing no normal gene version remains (all schematic).

scenes.tts: So experimenters do not judge by count or chromosome size alone. They check what DNA was gained or lost, trace breaks with probes, and test which gene versions remain. Chromosome painting has a limit too. Painted territories press together like yarn, with loose loops poking into neighbours. Whole-nucleus painting maps those territories, not whether edges mix.

scenes.visual: Three crisp labels appear in sequence beside the schematic spread—'DNA gained or lost', 'Breaks', 'Gene versions'—as fluorescent probes pinpoint a breakpoint and check which gene versions remain on the pairs; the spread then refolds into the painted schematic nucleus where coloured territories press together like balls of yarn, and a close-up at a glowing border shows loose loops poking across with a label: 'Whole-nucleus paint: edges unresolved (schematic)'.

scenes.tts: These methods unlocked three landmark discoveries. In 1959, Jérôme Lejeune, Marthe Gautier, and Raymond Turpin counted chromosomes in nine children with Down syndrome. Their cultured cells held forty-seven chromosomes, not forty-six. That extra chromosome, later numbered twenty-one, tied chromosome content to the condition.
scenes.caption: These methods unlocked three landmark discoveries. In 1959, Jérôme Lejeune, Marthe Gautier, and Raymond Turpin counted chromosomes in nine children with Down syndrome. Their cultured cells held 47 chromosomes, not 46. That extra chromosome, later numbered 21, tied chromosome content to the condition.
scenes.visual: The schematic karyotype spread returns with a bold year tag '1959' and label 'Down syndrome'; the chromosome counter steps from 46 to 47 as a third glowing copy slides smoothly beside pair 21 (counts 46 and 47 given; rod shapes schematic).

scenes.tts: In 1960, Peter Nowell and David Hungerford saw a small chromosome in chronic myeloid leukaemia blood cells. In 1973, Janet Rowley showed it was chromosome twenty-two, its missing piece attached to chromosome nine. Later work tied that join to the fusion of two genes, B C R and A B L.
scenes.caption: In 1960, Peter Nowell and David Hungerford saw a small chromosome in chronic myeloid leukaemia blood cells. In 1973, Janet Rowley showed it was chromosome 22, its missing piece attached to chromosome 9. Later work tied that join to the fusion of two genes, BCR and ABL.
scenes.visual: On the same schematic spread, year tag '1960' spotlights a small, visibly shortened chromosome, which year tag '1973' then labels as chromosome 22; the missing coloured piece of chromosome 22 then glows at the tip of chromosome 9, and the junction brightens with the label 'BCR–ABL fusion (schematic)'.

scenes.tts: In 1963, James Till, Ernest McCulloch, and Andrew Becker tracked marrow cells injected into irradiated mice. Chromosome markers showed each spleen colony was a clone, grown from one cell. Counting, banding and painting chromosomes make number, rearrangements and lineage visible.
scenes.caption: In 1963, James Till, Ernest McCulloch, and Andrew Becker tracked marrow cells injected into irradiated mice. Chromosome markers showed each spleen colony was a clone, grown from one cell. Counting, banding and painting chromosomes make number, rearrangements and lineage visible.
scenes.visual: Year tag '1963' appears as one schematic nucleus carrying one distinctive marker chromosome (a stained rod with an odd shape, not a fluorescent label) divides into an expanding cluster of daughter cells all bearing that same marker chromosome, labelled 'One cell, one clone (schematic)'; the camera then pulls smoothly back to unite the film's one world: countable pairs, glowing swapped pieces, and a mapped nucleus.

scenes.visual: Clean high-contrast end card over the softly dimming glowing schematic nucleus, displaying the take-home rule verbatim in large text: 'Stained spreads and fluorescent probes expose chromosome number, rearrangements, and territories.'
